title: Kolibri 1.1: More Efficient. More Capable. — Aleph Alpha
excerpt: Kolibri 1.1 is our improved English-German open-weight model: a new sparse-attention architecture makes it faster and cheaper per task, and it is stronger at agentic work, grounding, citations and safety.
content_html:
Research

Aleph Alpha

23/11/2026

Seven weeks ago we released Kolibri 1.0, our sovereign open-weight English-German model. Today, we release an improved Kolibri 1.1 taking into account customer and community feedback. The weights are available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license terms.

Kolibri 1.1 introduces a new sparse-attention architecture and more efficient reasoning. These make it faster and cheaper to run, needing 3.4 times less GPU time per task than Kolibri 1.0 while achieving a higher overall score (defined on the model card). By this overall score, it is the strongest model in its weight class (3–4B active parameters) in both English and German, and it even surpasses the larger GPT-OSS 120B, Mistral Small 4 and Nemotron 3 Super. Compared with Kolibri 1.0, Kolibri 1.1 improves on efficiency, agentic coding and search, instruction following, visual output, grounding, citations, prompt-injection resistance and German–English translation, and it hallucinates less. Kolibri 1.1 also runs on a wider range of hardware from day one, with official quantized builds and vLLM and transformers support.

Kolibri at a glance

Like Kolibri 1.0, Kolibri 1.1 is an English-German Mixture-of-Experts model of similar size, with 75B total and 3B active parameters and a context window of up to 1M tokens. We built Kolibri 1.1 on the same pre-trained model as Kolibri 1.0 and improved mid- and post-training. It uses our new sparse-attention architecture from mid-training onward. We densified the first layers, bringing the model down to 75B total parameters compared to 78B for Kolibri 1.0. Kolibri 1.0's defining strengths carry over to Kolibri 1.1:

  • Efficient by design. Kolibri sits on the Pareto frontier of quality versus serving cost in English and German, and is small enough to run on-premise.
  • Native German. A bilingual German/English tokenizer and a pre-training mix with 21.3% of its tokens in German make Kolibri bilingual by design.
  • Contextualized performance. Trained on internal data that mirrors real enterprise and government workflows, and evaluated on separate, held-out customer-proxy suites, Kolibri shows competitive performance on these tasks.
  • Grounded answers. Kolibri trained with abstention data and our Merlin-Arthur protocol to say "I don't know" when its context does not support an answer. It leads all compared models on the M/A grounding score.
  • Sovereign and compliant. Built in Germany, trained in Germany and Finland under European law, with full control of the pipeline from data to evaluation, and developed in line with the European legal framework, especially the EU AI Act, the GPAI Code of Practice, GDPR and copyright law.

On our benchmark category averages, Kolibri 1.1 scores higher than Kolibri 1.0 in math and knowledge in both English and German, and in code, engineering, instruction following, grounding, long context, safety, and translation. On the AA-Omniscience Index, which rewards correct answers and penalizes wrong guesses, it more than halves the gap between wrong and correct answers compared with Kolibri 1.0. Across our benchmarks, Kolibri 1.1 uses 41% fewer output tokens per task on average. It also handles long contexts better: at 1M tokens of context, our sparse-attention architecture lets it generate up to 14 times more output tokens per second per GPU than Kolibri 1.0.

Read our launch post and detailed tech report explaining how we built Kolibri 1.0.

What's new in Kolibri 1.1

Faster and cheaper per task

We introduce an improved model architecture and more efficient reasoning, which together make each task faster and more cost-effective to run.

Lower serving cost. Kolibri 1.1 introduces a custom sparse attention recipe that significantly accelerates inference as context length increases, without compromising model quality. Kolibri 1.1's decode throughput on four B300s is up to 14× faster than Kolibri 1.0 at a context length of one million tokens. Simultaneously, each request requires less memory so that the same GPUs serve three times as many concurrent requests. The result is more efficient serving for long-context workloads such as agentic workflows and processing large documents or codebases.

At its core, our sparse attention architecture allows each token to attend to the 2,048 most relevant tokens, plus the 128 most recent ones. Relevance is measured by how well a token's key matches the current query: first on summaries of 16-token blocks, then on the individual tokens of the best blocks. Layers also share their KV cache, further reducing memory requirements. We will explain our architecture in detail in an upcoming blog post later this week.

Fewer tokens per task. Besides architecture efficiency, the key component driving the model's cost is the number of tokens spent reasoning per task. The fewer tokens a model needs to reason about a task, the lower the cost and latency for an answer. We have significantly improved reasoning efficiency, so that Kolibri 1.1 uses 41% fewer output tokens per task when aggregated the same way as our overall model card scores. Below we compare the aggregate benchmark score against the aggregated number of tokens each model uses at their highest reasoning level: Kolibri 1.1 sits on the Pareto frontier, i.e., no model in this plot scores higher while using fewer tokens.

More efficient reasoning at every effort. As with Kolibri 1.0, the reasoning effort of Kolibri 1.1 is set per request, from none to high, trading answer quality against cost and latency. Kolibri 1.1 needs fewer tokens at every level, from 3.6 times fewer at low effort to 1.8 times fewer at high effort, so the low settings now save real cost and latency. Together with faster serving, this makes Kolibri 1.1 much better suited to latency-sensitive tasks.

Stronger at real work

Agentic tasks. We've significantly expanded our agentic post-training suite. As a result, Kolibri 1.1 now handles longer tasks, writes better code, and searches more effectively. In coding, it improves on SWE-Bench Verified (64.0% → 70.4%) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (25.8% → 35.6%). The largest gains are in agentic search and retrieval: BrowseComp-Plus (33.1% → 43.9%), our German Agentic Wikipedia QA benchmark (63.9% → 73.7%) and MuSiQue (78.3% → 86.4%). On all three, Kolibri 1.1 leads its weight class by 8 to 19 points, and outperforms the larger models GPT-OSS 120B, Mistral Small 4, and Nemotron 3 Super.

Built for real enterprise work. Our customer-proxy suites mirror real workflows in sectors such as the German public sector, aerospace and industrial manufacturing. On our two largest suites, Kolibri 1.1 scores highest among models with 3–4B active parameters: 86.0% in the German public sector (next best: Kolibri 1.0 with 77.0%) and 68.7% in aerospace (next best: again Kolibri 1.0, at 64.9%). The smaller suites move by a few points either way, within their sampling noise.

Visual output. One common request from the community was better visual output. While Kolibri 1.1 is still a text-only model, it now writes better code that renders visuals, such as SVG graphics and web animations. This is reflected in BenchCAD, which measures CAD manipulation and schematics for industrial use cases: Kolibri 1.1 scores 21 points higher on average than Kolibri 1.0. The difference also shows when we ask our model to generate SVGs:

Safer and more trustworthy

Fewer hallucinations. We trained Kolibri to abstain when the context does not support an answer. Kolibri 1.1 improves in grounding, reduces hallucinations and is better at citing its sources. When it doesn't know the answer on AA-Omniscience, the key hallucination benchmark, it says so or gives a partial answer instead of guessing in 61.1% of cases, up from 42.1% for Kolibri 1.0. Its M/A grounding score, which measures how much of an answer provably comes from the source document, rises from 26.8 to 34.8, the highest of all compared models.

Better citations. During our evaluations, we saw that Kolibri 1.1 is better than Kolibri 1.0 and the other baselines at citing the passages it relies on: on a held-out test split of Nemotron Citation Following (extended with customer citation formats and an answer-correctness judge), 89.1% of its answers are both correct and cite exactly the supporting passages, with no missing or irrelevant sources. That is up from 67.7% for Kolibri 1.0 and on par with the best compared models.

Safety. Kolibri 1.1 is more robust against prompt injection. On AgentDojo, where attacks are hidden in tool outputs, it resists 99.1% of injection attempts, up from 30.3% for Kolibri 1.0. On CyberSecEval 2, where attacks are hidden in the user prompt, it resists 93.2% (Kolibri 1.0: 85.3%), the highest of all compared models.

Better at English ↔ German translations

Kolibri 1.1 translates more accurately, reaching a MetricX error of 2.8 from German to English and 1.8 from English to German on the WMT24++ benchmark, down from 3.0 and 2.2 for Kolibri 1.0 (lower is better).

Runs locally

Kolibri 1.1 has vLLM support from day one through our official plug-in and Hugging Face transformers support, which acts as a reference for community implementations. For local experimentation, it now ships with official GGUF quantizations and a llama.cpp implementation supporting CPU, NVIDIA CUDA, and Apple Metal backends. The smallest build runs on GPUs with 24 GB of VRAM. Details on getting started are on the model card.

How we built it in 7 weeks

Kolibri 1.1 is the result of a 7-week iteration cycle following the release of Kolibri 1.0. After launch, we collected feedback from customers, the online community, and our go-to-market teams, and prioritized new features based on impact and effort. Each prioritized item then became two things: a benchmark that measures the problem, and new training data or environments that address it. As for Kolibri 1.0, these training environments are synthetic and kept apart from the evaluation items, so we improved Kolibri against our benchmarks without training on customer data. Teams contributed to the same model factory pipeline and owned each capability end to end, from data to evaluation.

Because our model factory evaluates every checkpoint automatically on benchmarks as it trains, teams saw within days whether a change helped, and whether it hurt anything else. That fast loop is what took us from launch feedback to a released model in seven weeks.

Benchmarks

We ran benchmarks with our own harnesses and the highest reasoning effort for all models, as for Kolibri 1.0. In the following table, Kolibri 1.1 is compared to Kolibri 1.0, several recent MoE models, and dense models. The best value in each row is in bold, and the best value of each weight class is underlined. Substantially larger baseline models are not included in the comparisons and greyed out.

Benchmarks are in English unless labelled (DE). If a similar benchmark is available in both languages, we explicitly mark the English one with (EN). Model names are shortened to the point where they still uniquely identify a model.

Get started

Kolibri 1.1 is available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. 

pip install "aleph-alpha-inference>=2"
vllm serve Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1.1 \
  --reasoning-parser kolibri1 \
  --tool-call-parser kolibri1 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice

Quantized builds are also available on Hugging Face. You can run with llama.cpp via: 

llama-server --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.99 --top-k 128 \
  -hf Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1.1-GGUF:Q4_K_M

Contact for deployment and specialization

Our team can help you deploy Kolibri 1.1 on your own infrastructure or access it through our Inference API, and specialize it for your domain: contact sales.

How we built it in 7 weeks Kolibri 1.1 is the result of a 7-week iteration cycle following the release of Kolibri 1.0. After launch, we collected feedback from customers, the online community, and our go-to-market teams, and prioritized new features based on impact and effort. Each prioritized item then became two things: a benchmark that measures the problem, and new training data or environments that address it. As for Kolibri 1.0, these training environments are synthetic and kept apart from the evaluation items, so we improved Kolibri against our benchmarks without training on customer data. Teams contributed to the same model factory pipeline and owned each capability end to end, from data to evaluation. Because our model factory evaluates every checkpoint automatically on benchmarks as it trains, teams saw within days whether a change helped, and whether it hurt anything else. That fast loop is what took us from launch feedback to a released model in seven weeks. blocks.html_en: Lower serving cost. Kolibri 1.1 introduces a custom sparse attention recipe that significantly accelerates inference as context length increases, without compromising model quality. Kolibri 1.1's decode throughput on four B300s is up to 14× faster than Kolibri 1.0 at a context length of one million tokens. Simultaneously, each request requires less memory so that the same GPUs serve three times as many concurrent requests. The result is more efficient serving for long-context workloads such as agentic workflows and processing large documents or codebases.

blocks.html_en: At its core, our sparse attention architecture allows each token to attend to the 2,048 most relevant tokens, plus the 128 most recent ones. Relevance is measured by how well a token's key matches the current query: first on summaries of 16-token blocks, then on the individual tokens of the best blocks. Layers also share their KV cache, further reducing memory requirements. We will explain our architecture in detail in an upcoming blog post later this week.

content_html_zh:
研究

阿莱夫·阿尔法

23/11/2026

Seven weeks ago we released Kolibri 1.0, our sovereign open-weight English-German model. Today, we release an improved Kolibri 1.1 taking into account customer and community feedback. The weights are available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license terms.

Kolibri 1.1 introduces a new sparse-attention architecture and more efficient reasoning. These make it faster and cheaper to run, needing 3.4 times less GPU time per task than Kolibri 1.0 while achieving a higher overall score (defined on the model card). By this overall score, it is the strongest model in its weight class (3–4B active parameters) in both English and German, and it even surpasses the larger GPT-OSS 120B, Mistral Small 4 and Nemotron 3 Super. Compared with Kolibri 1.0, Kolibri 1.1 improves on efficiency, agentic coding and search, instruction following, visual output, grounding, citations, prompt-injection resistance and German–English translation, and it hallucinates less. Kolibri 1.1 also runs on a wider range of hardware from day one, with official quantized builds and vLLM and transformers support.

Kolibri at a glance

Like Kolibri 1.0, Kolibri 1.1 is an English-German Mixture-of-Experts model of similar size, with 75B total and 3B active parameters and a context window of up to 1M tokens. We built Kolibri 1.1 on the same pre-trained model as Kolibri 1.0 and improved mid- and post-training. It uses our new sparse-attention architecture from mid-training onward. We densified the first layers, bringing the model down to 75B total parameters compared to 78B for Kolibri 1.0. Kolibri 1.0's defining strengths carry over to Kolibri 1.1:

  • Efficient by design. Kolibri sits on the Pareto frontier of quality versus serving cost in English and German, and is small enough to run on-premise.
  • Native German. A bilingual German/English tokenizer and a pre-training mix with 21.3% of its tokens in German make Kolibri bilingual by design.
  • Contextualized performance. Trained on internal data that mirrors real enterprise and government workflows, and evaluated on separate, held-out customer-proxy suites, Kolibri shows competitive performance on these tasks.
  • 接地气的答案。 Kolibri trained with abstention data and our Merlin-Arthur protocol to say "I don't know" when its context does not support an answer. It leads all compared models on the M/A grounding score.
  • Sovereign and compliant. Built in Germany, trained in Germany and Finland under European law, with full control of the pipeline from data to evaluation, and developed in line with the European legal framework, especially the EU AI Act, the GPAI Code of Practice, GDPR and copyright law.

On our benchmark category averages, Kolibri 1.1 scores higher than Kolibri 1.0 in math and knowledge in both English and German, and in code, engineering, instruction following, grounding, long context, safety, and translation. On the AA-Omniscience Index, which rewards correct answers and penalizes wrong guesses, it more than halves the gap between wrong and correct answers compared with Kolibri 1.0. Across our benchmarks, Kolibri 1.1 uses 41% fewer output tokens per task on average. It also handles long contexts better: at 1M tokens of context, our sparse-attention architecture lets it generate up to 14 times more output tokens per second per GPU than Kolibri 1.0.

Read our launch post and detailed tech report explaining how we built Kolibri 1.0.

What's new in Kolibri 1.1

Faster and cheaper per task

We introduce an improved model architecture and more efficient reasoning, which together make each task faster and more cost-effective to run.

Lower serving cost. Kolibri 1.1 introduces a custom sparse attention recipe that significantly accelerates inference as context length increases, without compromising model quality. Kolibri 1.1's decode throughput on four B300s is up to 14× faster than Kolibri 1.0 at a context length of one million tokens. Simultaneously, each request requires less memory so that the same GPUs serve three times as many concurrent requests. The result is more efficient serving for long-context workloads such as agentic workflows and processing large documents or codebases.

At its core, our sparse attention architecture allows each token to attend to the 2,048 most relevant tokens, plus the 128 most recent ones. Relevance is measured by how well a token's key matches the current query: first on summaries of 16-token blocks, then on the individual tokens of the best blocks. Layers also share their KV cache, further reducing memory requirements. We will explain our architecture in detail in an upcoming blog post later this week.

Fewer tokens per task. Besides architecture efficiency, the key component driving the model's cost is the number of tokens spent reasoning per task. The fewer tokens a model needs to reason about a task, the lower the cost and latency for an answer. We have significantly improved reasoning efficiency, so that Kolibri 1.1 uses 41% fewer output tokens per task when aggregated the same way as our overall model card scores. Below we compare the aggregate benchmark score against the aggregated number of tokens each model uses at their highest reasoning level: Kolibri 1.1 sits on the Pareto frontier, i.e., no model in this plot scores higher while using fewer tokens.

More efficient reasoning at every effort. As with Kolibri 1.0, the reasoning effort of Kolibri 1.1 is set per request, from none to high, trading answer quality against cost and latency. Kolibri 1.1 needs fewer tokens at every level, from 3.6 times fewer at low effort to 1.8 times fewer at high effort, so the low settings now save real cost and latency. Together with faster serving, this makes Kolibri 1.1 much better suited to latency-sensitive tasks.

Stronger at real work

Agentic tasks. We've significantly expanded our agentic post-training suite. As a result, Kolibri 1.1 now handles longer tasks, writes better code, and searches more effectively. In coding, it improves on SWE-Bench Verified (64.0% → 70.4%) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (25.8% → 35.6%). The largest gains are in agentic search and retrieval: BrowseComp-Plus (33.1% → 43.9%), our German Agentic Wikipedia QA benchmark (63.9% → 73.7%) and MuSiQue (78.3% → 86.4%). On all three, Kolibri 1.1 leads its weight class by 8 to 19 points, and outperforms the larger models GPT-OSS 120B, Mistral Small 4, and Nemotron 3 Super.

Built for real enterprise work. Our customer-proxy suites mirror real workflows in sectors such as the German public sector, aerospace and industrial manufacturing. On our two largest suites, Kolibri 1.1 scores highest among models with 3–4B active parameters: 86.0% in the German public sector (next best: Kolibri 1.0 with 77.0%) and 68.7% in aerospace (next best: again Kolibri 1.0, at 64.9%). The smaller suites move by a few points either way, within their sampling noise.

Visual output. One common request from the community was better visual output. While Kolibri 1.1 is still a text-only model, it now writes better code that renders visuals, such as SVG graphics and web animations. This is reflected in BenchCAD, which measures CAD manipulation and schematics for industrial use cases: Kolibri 1.1 scores 21 points higher on average than Kolibri 1.0. The difference also shows when we ask our model to generate SVGs:

Safer and more trustworthy

Fewer hallucinations. We trained Kolibri to abstain when the context does not support an answer. Kolibri 1.1 improves in grounding, reduces hallucinations and is better at citing its sources. When it doesn't know the answer on AA-Omniscience, the key hallucination benchmark, it says so or gives a partial answer instead of guessing in 61.1% of cases, up from 42.1% for Kolibri 1.0. Its M/A grounding score, which measures how much of an answer provably comes from the source document, rises from 26.8 to 34.8, the highest of all compared models.

Better citations. During our evaluations, we saw that Kolibri 1.1 is better than Kolibri 1.0 and the other baselines at citing the passages it relies on: on a held-out test split of Nemotron Citation Following (extended with customer citation formats and an answer-correctness judge), 89.1% of its answers are both correct and cite exactly the supporting passages, with no missing or irrelevant sources. That is up from 67.7% for Kolibri 1.0 and on par with the best compared models.

安全。 Kolibri 1.1 is more robust against prompt injection. On AgentDojo, where attacks are hidden in tool outputs, it resists 99.1% of injection attempts, up from 30.3% for Kolibri 1.0. On CyberSecEval 2, where attacks are hidden in the user prompt, it resists 93.2% (Kolibri 1.0: 85.3%), the highest of all compared models.

Better at English ↔ German translations

Kolibri 1.1 translates more accurately, reaching a MetricX error of 2.8 from German to English and 1.8 from English to German on the WMT24++ benchmark, down from 3.0 and 2.2 for Kolibri 1.0 (lower is better).

Runs locally

Kolibri 1.1 has vLLM support from day one through our official plug-in and Hugging Face transformers support, which acts as a reference for community implementations. For local experimentation, it now ships with official GGUF quantizations and a llama.cpp implementation supporting CPU, NVIDIA CUDA, and Apple Metal backends. The smallest build runs on GPUs with 24 GB of VRAM. Details on getting started are on the model card.

How we built it in 7 weeks

Kolibri 1.1 is the result of a 7-week iteration cycle following the release of Kolibri 1.0. After launch, we collected feedback from customers, the online community, and our go-to-market teams, and prioritized new features based on impact and effort. Each prioritized item then became two things: a benchmark that measures the problem, and new training data or environments that address it. As for Kolibri 1.0, these training environments are synthetic and kept apart from the evaluation items, so we improved Kolibri against our benchmarks without training on customer data. Teams contributed to the same model factory pipeline and owned each capability end to end, from data to evaluation.

Because our model factory evaluates every checkpoint automatically on benchmarks as it trains, teams saw within days whether a change helped, and whether it hurt anything else. That fast loop is what took us from launch feedback to a released model in seven weeks.
